Revision, 26 September 2026

Revised analysis: some results below are superseded

A fully nested re-analysis (all tuning and selection inside grouped folds), a frozen sentinel test on May–August 2018 and new robustness checks changed several conclusions. The manuscript and results/revision/ hold the current numbers.

  • THMFP roughly doubled in May–August 2018 versus 2017 (×1.94 at 95% of sites) while HAAFP was unchanged and TOC rose 12%. Water-quality predictors failed for THMFP in this period (R² ≈ 0), and 90% intervals covered only 53–56% of observations. An analytical cause has not been ruled out.
  • The sentinel benefit is smaller than stated in section 6. With sentinels frozen on earlier months, four to eight sentinels raised THMFP R² for summer 2018 to 0.27–0.33; random sites did as well as optimized ones; HAAFP did not benefit.
  • Humic substances add information beyond TOC, most for HAAFP (ΔR² ≈ 0.09); organic carbon tracks change within sites (ρ ≈ 0.5).
  • Treatment removes HAA-forming carbon selectively: carbon-normalized HAAFP falls 53–56% versus 14–34% for THMFP. The earlier statement that ozonation raised formation potential at Bansong came from an incorrect stage order (pre-ozonation precedes settling).
1 · The data

A complete monthly panel over four kinds of water

Every sampling point has exactly one row per month. Eighteen water-quality inputs are grouped into field measurements (Temp, pH, Turbidity, EC, DO, SS), lab measurements (Br, BOD, COD, NH3-N, TOC, SUVA, Aromaticity, Mol. weight) and LC-OCD carbon fractions (Biopolymer, Humic substances, Building blocks, LMW neutrals). The outputs are trihalomethane and haloacetic-acid formation potentials in mg/L.

2 · Key EDA findings

Organic carbon quantity, season and place

  • Both targets are log-normal (medians 0.08 mg/L, range 0.007–0.55) and correlate with each other at Spearman 0.67. All modelling is on log10.
  • Humic substances and TOC are the strongest predictors: Spearman 0.66–0.78 with the targets. Bromide is weak on its own (≈0.2) and adds little once TOC is known.
  • Site and month each explain more variance than any single predictor: site η² up to 0.59 for HAAFP, date η² up to 0.47 for THMFP on river rows. A random train/test split would leak both.
  • River water carries about twice the formation potential of reservoirs and treated water. Along the main stem, values rise downstream and peak around the Goryeong reach in summer.
  • Treatment removes roughly half at coagulation/settling, ozonation slightly raises it, and GAC or F/A brings finished water to 0.03–0.05 mg/L.
  • Summer 2018 is anomalous: main-stem monthly medians reached 0.32 mg/L against ≤0.21 in every other month, and one tributary event (Hoecheon, Aug 2018) holds record values for several variables.
  • Data-quality handling: 29 Korean non-detect strings set to NaN with flags, 4 zero placeholders in the UV/size trio removed, blank site codes for two treatment trains recovered from names.
3 · Modelling

Three feature tiers, four ways of holding data out

Features were added in nested tiers so the value of each kind of information could be measured. Every model was tuned by a nested random search whose inner folds share the outer scheme's grouping, so held-out months and sites never leak into tuning. Ridge, HistGradientBoosting and XGBoost were compared against median, site-median and persistence baselines.

4 · Best models

One recommendation per target

Selection rule fixed before the experiments: the highest mean R² over the month and site schemes. Both winners are ridge regressions on network-aware features; the round-0 XGBoost models are kept in models/ for the chemistry-only case.

5 · Why ridge beat XGBoost

A linear model won because the task became one of propagating a measured shift

In round 0 the tree model led on unseen sites, where the job was to learn site-specific nonlinearities. Round 1 added the network's same-month values, and with them the strongest signal became a shift that has to be carried through to the prediction. That is a linear job, and it exposed a structural limit of trees.

  • Trees cannot predict beyond the training range. A boosted tree returns a constant inside each leaf, so its output never exceeds the largest value it was trained on. In the forward holdout one in ten THMFP observations sits above the training maximum of 0.29 mg/L. XGBoost tops out at 0.15 mg/L there and under-predicts those points by about a factor of four; ridge keeps extending along its slope, reaches 0.38 mg/L, and halves that error.
  • The gap is concentrated in anomalous months. Within the leave-months-out scheme the two models are close on typical months. On the high months of 2018 ridge still explains part of the variance while XGBoost explains almost none.
  • The new features are nearly linear in the log target. Ridge spreads its weight almost evenly across the group mean, basin mean, site encoding and last month's value, so when the whole basin rises every input pushes the prediction up together. A tree must rediscover each of those as step functions from about 500 rows.
  • Strong regularisation suits a small, collinear sample. Ridge chose a heavy penalty and the inputs are highly correlated (TOC with humic substances 0.78, humic substances with building blocks 0.81). Shrinking correlated coefficients together is what ridge does well; the trees show the larger fold-to-fold spread.
  • XGBoost still wins on unseen sites inside known months. With all feature blocks it reaches site R² 0.75 for THMFP against 0.68 for ridge, so the tree model stays the recommendation for a new site in a known period.

Anomalous months are those whose basin-wide median THMFP exceeds 0.15 mg/L (176 of 693 rows). Two caveats: the ridge pipeline also gained a missing-value indicator in round 1, which raised its own baseline, and the forward test rests on a single anomalous summer. Monotone constraints or a ridge–tree blend would likely narrow the gap; both were outside this round's scope.

6 · Sentinel sampling

Lab-test a few sites, predict the rest

The best models above need THMFP and HAAFP measured at most other sites in the same month, which makes them gap-fillers. They work because the basin moves together: 57 % of THMFP's month-to-month variation within a site is shared across all sites that month (HAAFP 36 %), and main-stem sites twelve steps apart still correlate at 0.72 for THMFP. A sentinel design exploits that signal at a fraction of the lab cost. Chemistry is measured everywhere, DBP only at k sentinel sites, and every other site is predicted from its chemistry, its normal level from this 16-month campaign, and how far the sentinels sit from their own normal level that month.

  • One sentinel recovers most of the benefit with 2 % of the lab tests; four to eight match full-network gap-filling for THMFP, and one or two are enough for HAAFP.
  • Useful sentinels differ by target. For HAAFP, Bansong raw water (M14) is chosen first in five of eight folds; for THMFP the first choice alternates between Namgang Reservoir and M14.
  • A QA screen is essential. Without it, one reading (Imha Reservoir, September 2017, THMFP 0.007 mg/L, the dataset minimum) dragged every site's prediction down by about a factor of three, and THMFP R² fell to 0.31 with two sentinels. Sentinel readings more than four robust SDs from the site's normal level are now dropped. The screen was added after seeing that failure, so the screened numbers are slightly optimistic.
  • Limits. Tested on new months only; a new site needs a calibration period. Treated-water stages are the weakest group. A fixed operational sentinel set still has to be chosen and validated on new data.
7 · Caveats

What to keep in mind

  • One seasonal cycle. Sixteen months is a single year plus four; the forward test is one anomalous summer. Expect degradation in unusual years and retrain as months arrive.
  • Network features need the network. Basin, group, downstream and plant-raw features assume the other sites were sampled the same month. Without them, fall back to the chemistry-only models.
  • Units are assumed (mg/L for the targets, µg/L C for LC-OCD fractions, µS/cm for EC); the workbook does not state them. Detection limits for the 29 non-detects are also unknown.
  • One model-side change slipped into round 1: ridge gained a missing-value indicator, which raised its own baseline. Feature gains are measured against the re-run baseline, so they are like-for-like.
  • Not yet tried: ridge–XGBoost blending, a joint two-target model, prediction intervals, robust losses.
Reproduce: uv sync → uv run python -m src.train --all → uv run python -m src.train --ablation → uv run python -m src.interpret. Notebooks notebooks/eda.ipynb and notebooks/modeling.ipynb render every figure. Repository: github.com/thanhtrunghuynh93/Korean_river.
